newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: U.S files show more disappeared in Honduras.
newsitem.headline: U.S files show more disappeared in Honduras.

text.p: U.S. documents show more people than previously thought may have "disappeared" at the hands of Honduran death squads who were helped by American and Argentine agents, the Honduran ombudsman said on Friday.

Ombudsman Leo Valladares said 2,600 pages of declassified files he received from the U.S. State Department showed more than the 184 documented cases of suspected leftists who disappeared in the 1980s and were believed killed by the army death squads.
"We found 'disappearances' that we didn't know about before," he told Reuters. "Just a few cases so far, but we continue screening the documents."

Valladares was now seeking access to Argentine files in a bid to prove his theory that Argentine military officers had an active and illegal role in the last decade in Honduras -- possibly training the military in torture and kidnapping tactics and performing such acts themselves.
"The military (in Honduras) deny any part (in human rights abuses) and are not providing any information," he added.

According to witnesses, Argentine soldiers did the "dirty work" for U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) agents in Honduras, he said. "They (the CIA agents) did not want to do things prohibited by their country's laws, so they used the Argentine military instead," Valladares said.
"Training included counterinsurgency manoeuvres and ... many actions which violated human rights, such as torture and the forced disappearance of people," he said.
But despite the 2,600 pages of documents, Washington has failed to provide him with more sensitive material.
The New York Times said in an editorial last week: "The Clinton administration has run out of reasonable excuses for its delay in assisting Valladares.

"So far only the State Department has turned over documents. The Defence Intelligence Agency and the CIA, which was more directly involved, are still reviewing their files. The CIA should also expedite its internal investigation, punish those who covered up crimes and release as complete a version as possible to the public."

The paper also urged Argentine President Carlos Menem to "keep his word" and give support to Valladares, who arrived on Wednesday to take part here in an international conference of ombudsmen next week. On Wednesday, Menem repeated his pledge to help in the investigation.

Valladares will seek meetings with Interior Minister Carlos Corach and army chief Gen. Martin Balza, who last year apologised for the army's human rights abuses during Argentina's 1976-1986 "dirty war" in which up to 30,000 people disappeared. He may also seek to talk with Menem.
"I assume they keep (files) closely guarded. But I do have hints of where documents can be found," Valladares said.
